prompt: When does the two-pointer technique apply, and what property of the input makes it valid?
reveal: Two pointers works when the array is sorted (or has some monotonic property) and you are searching for a pair/triple satisfying a condition. Validity rests on monotonicity: moving the left pointer right only increases the sum, moving the right pointer left only decreases it — so at each step you can eliminate an entire row or column of the search space without checking it. That is what turns O(n²) into O(n).

prompt: Fixed-size sliding window: state the invariant and why it is O(n) not O(nk).
reveal: The invariant is that the window always holds exactly k consecutive elements and you maintain its aggregate incrementally. Each step adds the entering element and removes the leaving one in O(1), so every element is added once and removed once — 2n operations total, hence O(n). Recomputing the aggregate from scratch each step would be the O(nk) naive version.

prompt: Variable-size sliding window (e.g. longest substring satisfying a constraint): describe the loop shape and when you shrink.
reveal: Outer loop expands the right edge one element at a time, always adding to the window state. An inner while loop shrinks from the left as long as the window VIOLATES the constraint. After shrinking, the window is valid, so record the answer. Each pointer only moves forward across the whole run, so it is O(n) despite the nested loop. The tell: "longest/shortest subarray such that ..." with a constraint that is monotone in window size.

prompt: Binary search on the ANSWER: what problem shape signals it, and what must be true of the predicate?
reveal: The signal is: "minimize the maximum ..." or "find the smallest capacity/speed/time such that X is feasible" — you are not searching an array, you are searching the answer space. The predicate feasible(x) must be MONOTONE: if x works, every larger x works (or vice versa). Then binary search the value range, calling feasible() as the test, giving O(log(range) × costOfCheck). Getting the monotonicity argument right is the whole problem; the binary search itself is boilerplate.

prompt: Write the invariant for lower_bound (first element >= target) and explain the classic off-by-one trap.
reveal: Invariant: the answer lies in [lo, hi], with everything left of lo strictly less than target and everything from hi onward >= target. Loop while lo < hi; mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2; if a[mid] >= target then hi = mid (keep mid, it is a candidate) else lo = mid+1 (mid is ruled out). The trap is writing hi = mid-1, which discards a valid answer, or using (lo+hi)/2 which can overflow. Terminating with lo == hi gives the answer position.

prompt: Prefix sums: give the core identity, and extend it to "count subarrays summing to k".
reveal: Identity: sum(i..j) = prefix[j+1] - prefix[i], so any range sum is O(1) after O(n) preprocessing. For counting subarrays summing to k, rewrite: prefix[j] - prefix[i] = k means prefix[i] = prefix[j] - k. So sweep j, and use a hash map of how many times each prefix value has been seen; add map[prefix[j]-k] to the answer, then record prefix[j]. O(n). The conceptual jump is turning a range question into a lookup of previously-seen prefix values.

prompt: Monotonic stack: what does it compute, what is in the stack, and why is it O(n) amortized?
reveal: It computes, for each element, the nearest element to the left (or right) that is smaller/larger — the basis of "next greater element," largest rectangle in histogram, daily temperatures, trapping rain water. The stack holds indices whose values form a monotonic sequence; before pushing i you pop everything that i invalidates, and each pop resolves an answer. Amortized O(n) because every index is pushed once and popped at most once — 2n operations total, even though a single step may pop many.

prompt: Top-k with a heap: which heap type do you use for the k LARGEST elements, and why is that counterintuitive choice correct?
reveal: Use a MIN-heap of size k. Counterintuitive, but correct: the min-heap root is the smallest of your current best k, so when a new element arrives you compare against the root and evict it if the newcomer is bigger. That keeps the k largest for O(n log k) instead of O(n log n) for a full sort. Mirror it for k smallest (max-heap). The rule: the heap root should be the element you are most willing to throw away.

prompt: Merging intervals and the "minimum meeting rooms" variant: what is the shared first move, and how do they diverge?

src.ref: Ch.6 Weighted graph algorithms / greedy scheduling

reveal: Shared first move: SORT by start time — nearly every interval problem begins there. Merging: sweep and merge the current interval with the next whenever next.start <= current.end, extending the end to max(ends). Minimum rooms: you need concurrency, not merging — so use a min-heap of end times; for each interval, pop any meeting that has ended, then push this end; the heap size at its peak is the answer. Alternatively sort starts and ends separately and sweep as +1/-1 events.

prompt: What is an exchange argument, and how do you use it to prove a greedy algorithm is correct?
reveal: An exchange argument proves greedy optimality by showing any optimal solution can be transformed into the greedy one without getting worse. Take an optimal solution that differs from greedy at the first decision point; swap that choice for greedy’s choice and show the result is still valid and no worse. By induction, greedy is optimal. Classic use: interval scheduling by earliest finish time — swapping any optimal’s first interval for the earliest-finishing one leaves at least as many remaining slots. If you cannot construct the exchange, greedy probably fails and you need DP.

prompt: Backtracking template: name the three parts of the recursion and the single most common bug.

src.ref: Ch.9 Combinatorial search and heuristic methods

reveal: Three parts: (1) a base case that records a complete solution, (2) a loop over candidate choices at this position, (3) choose → recurse → UNCHOOSE (undo the state change). The most common bug is forgetting to undo — mutating shared state (a visited array, a path list) on the way down and never restoring it on the way up, so later branches see contaminated state. The second most common: appending the path by reference so all recorded solutions alias the same object; copy it when recording.

prompt: How do you convert a recursive solution into a DP? State the two questions that define any DP.
reveal: The two questions are: (1) What is the STATE — the minimal set of parameters that fully describes a subproblem? (2) What is the TRANSITION — how does the answer for a state combine answers of smaller states? Once you have those, memoize the recursion (top-down) or fill a table in dependency order (bottom-up). The complexity is (number of states) × (work per transition). If the state has parameters that do not affect future decisions, you can drop them — that is the main compression trick.

prompt: 0/1 knapsack: give the state, transition, and how to reduce the table from 2D to 1D. Why does the 1D loop run backwards?
reveal: State: dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items within capacity w. Transition: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w] (skip), value[i] + dp[i-1][w-weight[i]] (take)). Since row i only depends on row i-1, keep one array. The inner capacity loop must run DOWNWARD (from W to weight[i]) so that dp[w-weight[i]] still holds the PREVIOUS row’s value — running upward would let the same item be taken multiple times, which silently turns it into the unbounded knapsack.

prompt: Longest increasing subsequence: give the O(n²) DP, then explain what the O(n log n) version’s array actually holds.
reveal: O(n²): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) over all j < i with a[j] < a[i]; answer is max(dp). O(n log n): maintain an array tails where tails[k] = the SMALLEST possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each element, binary search for the first tail >= it and overwrite (or append if larger than all). Crucially, tails is NOT the actual subsequence — only its LENGTH is the answer. Keeping tails minimal is what leaves the most room for future extensions.

prompt: 2D grid DP (paths, edit distance): what determines the fill order, and how do you handle the boundary?
reveal: Fill order must respect dependencies: if dp[i][j] depends on dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1], iterate rows top-to-bottom and columns left-to-right so both are already computed. Boundaries are the base cases — first row/column usually have only one predecessor, so either initialize them explicitly or pad the table with a sentinel row/column (index shifted by 1) so the general formula applies everywhere without special-casing. The padding trick removes most off-by-one bugs.

prompt: Give the three DFS traversal orders and one problem each is uniquely suited to.
reveal: Preorder (node, left, right) — serializing/cloning a tree, since you see the parent before children. Inorder (left, node, right) — on a BST this emits sorted order, so it validates a BST or finds the kth smallest. Postorder (left, right, node) — anything where children must be resolved first: computing height, deleting a tree, evaluating an expression tree, or bottom-up aggregation.

prompt: How do you validate a BST, and why is "check each node against its two children" wrong?
reveal: Checking only against immediate children is wrong because the BST property is global, not local: every node in the left subtree must be less than the ancestor, not merely less than its parent. A node can satisfy its parent yet violate a grandparent. Correct approach: recurse carrying a (min, max) range — each node must lie strictly inside it, and the range narrows as you descend. Alternative: an inorder traversal must produce a strictly increasing sequence.

prompt: When is a trie the right structure over a hash map, and what is its cost profile?
reveal: A trie wins when you need PREFIX operations: autocomplete, "does any word start with X," longest common prefix, or word-search-on-a-grid where you prune dead branches early. A hash map gives O(1) exact lookup but cannot answer prefix questions without scanning everything. Trie costs O(L) per operation where L is word length (independent of the number of words), at the price of significant memory — one node per character per distinct prefix, each with a child map.

prompt: Fast/slow pointers: prove why they meet if a linked list has a cycle, and describe finding the cycle START.
reveal: If a cycle exists, the fast pointer (2 steps) gains exactly 1 step per iteration on the slow pointer (1 step). Once both are inside the cycle, the gap closes by one each round, so it must hit zero — they meet. To find the cycle start (Floyd): after they meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance BOTH one step at a time; they meet at the cycle entrance. This falls out of the algebra: the distance from head to entrance equals the distance from meeting point to entrance, modulo cycle length.

prompt: What does it mean for a sort to be stable, and give a case where it matters.
reveal: A stable sort preserves the relative order of records that compare equal. It matters when you sort by multiple keys in passes: to sort employees by department then by name, you sort by name FIRST, then by department — stability keeps the name order intact within each department. It is also required for radix sort to work. Note that std::sort is NOT stable; std::stable_sort is.

prompt: Explain amortized analysis using dynamic array (vector) growth. Why is push_back O(1) amortized despite occasional O(n) resizes?
reveal: Doubling capacity means a resize copying n elements happens only after n cheap pushes. Summing the cost of resizes over n insertions gives n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n — a geometric series bounded by a constant multiple of n. Divided across n operations, that is O(1) per operation on average, even though any single push may cost O(n). The key is that the expensive operation PAYS FOR the cheap ones that preceded it (the accounting method). Growing by a constant amount instead of a factor would break this and give O(n) amortized.

prompt: State the complexity of: hash map lookup worst case, heap push, binary search, and sorting n items. Which of these do people most often state wrong?
reveal: Hash map lookup: O(1) average but O(n) WORST case (all keys colliding) — this is the one most often stated wrong; interviewers probe it. Heap push/pop: O(log n). Binary search: O(log n). Comparison sorting: O(n log n) lower bound. Also worth having ready: building a heap from an array is O(n), not O(n log n).

prompt: What is a Turing machine, and why is it THE model of computation rather than one arbitrary choice?

src.ref: Turing machine as model of computation

reveal: A Turing machine is a finite-state control with an unbounded tape and a read/write head: each step reads the scanned symbol, and based on it plus the current state, writes a symbol, moves left/right, and changes state, until it halts accepting or rejecting (or loops forever). It matters because of the Church-Turing thesis: every 'effective procedure' any physical computer or algorithm can carry out is computable by some TM. It is robust — multi-tape machines, random-access (RAM) models, and modern languages all compute the same functions, and simulate each other with at most polynomial overhead, so 'polynomial time' is a model-independent notion. That robustness is exactly what lets us talk about intrinsic difficulty of a problem rather than difficulty on one machine.

prompt: What does it mean for the halting problem to be undecidable, and what is the diagonalization idea that proves it?
reveal: Undecidable means NO algorithm exists — not that it is slow, but that no Turing machine can, for every pair (program M, input w), always halt and correctly report whether M halts on w. The proof is self-reference: assume a decider H(M,w) exists. Build D that takes a program's own code <M>, runs H(<M>,<M>), and then does the OPPOSITE — it loops if H says M halts on itself, and halts if H says it loops. Now ask what D does on its own code <D>: whatever H predicts, D contradicts it. So H cannot exist. The lesson for an engineer: some perfectly well-defined questions (does this code terminate? are these two programs equivalent?) have no general algorithm at all, regardless of compute — by Rice's theorem, essentially every non-trivial semantic property of programs is undecidable.

prompt: What is a many-one (mapping) reduction A ≤ B, and how do you use one to prove a problem is hard? Which direction is the classic mistake?
reveal: A ≤ B is a computable function f that maps each instance x of A to an instance f(x) of B such that x is a YES for A exactly when f(x) is a YES for B. It says 'B is at least as hard as A': any solver for B, composed with f, solves A. So hardness flows from A to B. For undecidability you use any computable f (halting problem ≤ your problem ⇒ your problem is undecidable); for NP-hardness you additionally require f to run in polynomial time (≤p), so that B ∈ P would give A ∈ P. The classic mistake is reversing the direction: to prove YOUR problem is hard you must reduce a KNOWN-hard problem TO yours (known ≤ yours), not yours to something known. Reducing yours to SAT only shows yours is easy (in NP), not hard.

prompt: State precisely what P and NP are, using the verifier definition of NP. What is the single most common misconception about NP?
reveal: P is the class of decision problems solvable by a deterministic algorithm in time polynomial in the input size. NP is the class where every YES-instance has a short (polynomial-size) CERTIFICATE that a deterministic verifier can check in polynomial time — e.g. for SAT the certificate is a satisfying assignment; for 'has a route under budget B' it is the route. Equivalently, NP is what a nondeterministic TM decides in polynomial time (guess the certificate, then verify). P ⊆ NP trivially. P vs NP asks whether every problem whose solutions are easy to CHECK is also easy to FIND. The big misconception: NP does not mean 'non-polynomial' or 'not in P' — many NP problems (all of P) are polynomial. NP is about efficient verifiability. Note the asymmetry: NP guarantees a certificate only for YES-instances; the mirror class for NO-instance certificates is coNP.

prompt: Define NP-complete, and give the IDEA (not the full proof) behind Cook-Levin showing SAT is NP-complete. Why does one such problem matter so much?
reveal: A problem is NP-complete if it is (1) in NP and (2) NP-hard — every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. Cook-Levin proves SAT qualifies. The idea: take ANY NP problem, given by a nondeterministic machine that would accept in poly time. Its computation can be laid out as a tableau — a grid whose rows are the machine's tape/head/state configuration at each of the polynomially-many time steps. You build a boolean formula with variables for each cell and clauses that force: a valid start row, that each row follows from the one above by a legal transition, and an accepting final row. That formula is satisfiable exactly when the machine has an accepting run. So SAT encodes all of NP. The payoff: because every NP problem reduces to SAT (and to any NP-complete problem), if a SINGLE NP-complete problem had a polynomial algorithm, then P = NP and thousands of problems collapse to easy at once.

prompt: In an interview, how do you argue that a new problem is NP-complete? Give the two-step recipe and how to pick the problem you reduce from.
reveal: Two steps. (1) Membership: show it is in NP by describing a polynomial-size certificate and a polynomial-time check (e.g. 'given a candidate subset, verify in O(n) that it sums to the target'). (2) Hardness: pick a KNOWN NP-complete problem and reduce IT to yours in polynomial time (known ≤p yours), showing your problem is at least as hard. Choose a known problem structurally close to yours: 3-SAT for logic/constraint problems, Clique / Independent Set / Vertex Cover for graph selection, Hamiltonian Path or TSP for ordering/routing, Subset-Sum or Partition for number/weight problems, 3-Coloring for assignment/conflict. The reduction must map YES to YES and NO to NO (a gadget construction). Practical tell: if a problem seems to require searching exponentially many combinations with no exploitable structure (monotonicity, optimal substructure, matroid), suspect it is NP-hard and look for the reduction.

prompt: Name the canonical NP-complete problems worth memorizing, and one relationship between two of them.
reveal: SAT and 3-SAT (satisfy a boolean / 3-CNF formula); Clique (k mutually adjacent vertices); Independent Set (k mutually non-adjacent vertices); Vertex Cover (k vertices touching every edge); Hamiltonian Path/Cycle (visit every vertex once); TSP-decision (a tour of length ≤ B); Subset-Sum and Partition (a subset hitting a target sum); Graph 3-Coloring; Knapsack-decision. They are all interreducible — each reduces to the others in polynomial time. Cleanest relationship: S is a Vertex Cover of graph G iff its complement V\S is an Independent Set, so the two are trivially inter-reducible and a k-vertex cover exists iff an (n−k)-independent-set exists.

prompt: Your problem is NP-hard but you still have to ship. What are the standard ways to cope, and what does each actually promise?
reveal: Approximation algorithms: run in polynomial time with a PROVABLE ratio to optimal — e.g. a 2-approximation for Vertex Cover, Christofides' 3/2 for metric TSP; but some problems (general TSP, Max-Clique) are inapproximable to any good factor unless P = NP. Heuristics / local search (greedy, simulated annealing, genetic): no guarantee, often excellent in practice. Exact but smarter than brute force: e.g. Held-Karp solves TSP in O(2^n n^2), far better than n!. Parameterized / FPT: exponential ONLY in a small parameter k, polynomial in n — Vertex Cover is roughly O(2^k · n), fine when k is small. Restrict the input: many NP-hard graph problems are polynomial on trees, planar, or bounded-treewidth graphs. Industrial solvers: SAT/ILP solvers are worst-case exponential but routinely crush real instances. The skill is matching the tactic to whether you need a guarantee, a small parameter, or just 'good enough fast.'

prompt: What is PSPACE, how do L and NL fit in, and what kind of problem is PSPACE-complete? Where do the classes sit relative to P and NP?
reveal: PSPACE is the problems solvable using polynomial WORK SPACE with no time limit — space is reusable, which makes it powerful. L is deterministic O(log n) work-tape space (input is read-only, so you cannot even store a copy), and NL is its nondeterministic version; think pointers and counters, e.g. graph reachability (STCON) is NL-complete. The known chain is L ⊆ NL ⊆ P ⊆ NP ⊆ PSPACE, and every one of those inclusions is believed but not proven strict (we only know L ≠ PSPACE via the hierarchy theorem). PSPACE-complete problems are the 'unbounded interaction' ones: TQBF / true quantified boolean formulas (∃x∀y∃z …), and generalized two-player games with a polynomially-bounded number of moves like Generalized Geography or Hex, where you must reason about all of the opponent's responses. (Games that can run for exponentially many moves — generalized Go, Chess, Checkers — jump up to EXPTIME-complete.) Rule of thumb: alternating ∃/∀ quantifiers or perfect-play games smell PSPACE, not merely NP.

prompt: What does Savitch's theorem say, what is its headline corollary, and what is the algorithmic trick behind it?
reveal: Savitch's theorem: NSPACE(s(n)) ⊆ DSPACE(s(n)^2) for s(n) ≥ log n. Headline corollary: NPSPACE = PSPACE (polynomial squared is still polynomial), and NL ⊆ DSPACE(log^2 n). The trick is a recursive divide-and-conquer on reachability: to test whether configuration A can reach B in at most 2^k steps, GUESS a midpoint configuration M and recursively check A→M in 2^(k-1) steps and M→B in 2^(k-1) steps. The recursion is only k levels deep, and each level stores one configuration of size O(s(n)), so total space is O(s(n) · k) = O(s(n)^2) — and it is deterministic because we can try all midpoints one at a time, reusing the space. The meaning: for SPACE, nondeterminism buys at most a quadratic advantage — a stark contrast with TIME, where nondeterminism (P vs NP) is believed to give an exponential gap.

prompt: What do the time and space hierarchy theorems tell us, and why do they matter given that P vs NP is open?
reveal: They say that more resource strictly buys more computational power. Time hierarchy: given more than roughly a logarithmic factor more time, you can decide strictly more languages — DTIME(f) ⊊ DTIME(g) when f(n)·log f(n) = o(g(n)). Space hierarchy: DSPACE(f) ⊊ DSPACE(g) whenever f(n) = o(g(n)). Both are proved by diagonalization: build a machine that uses the larger budget to simulate every machine of the smaller budget and deliberately disagree with each, so its language is decidable within the larger budget but not the smaller. Why it matters: these give UNCONDITIONAL separations that P vs NP lacks — they prove, for example, P ⊊ EXPTIME and L ⊊ PSPACE outright. So we know for certain that harder-than-P problems exist and that the complexity world does not collapse; the open questions (like P vs NP) are about the relationships the hierarchy theorems cannot reach, because those compare different MODES (determinism vs nondeterminism, time vs space), not the same resource at two levels.

prompt: Immerman-Szelepcsenyi: what surprising fact does it establish about nondeterministic space, and what is the technique? Why is it surprising next to what we believe about NP?
reveal: It proves NL = coNL — nondeterministic logspace is closed under complement. Concretely, NON-reachability ('vertex t is NOT reachable from s') is in NL, even though certifying the ABSENCE of a path naively looks like it needs to rule out all paths (a universal, coNP-flavored quantifier). The technique is inductive counting: nondeterministically compute the EXACT count of vertices reachable from s within i steps, building it up from the count for i−1. Once you know the true number R of reachable vertices, you can certify that t is unreachable by nondeterministically enumerating exactly R reachable vertices (each verified by guessing its path) and checking that t is not among them — all with only counters and pointers in logspace. It is surprising because the analogous question for TIME, whether NP = coNP, is believed FALSE: we think there is no short certificate that a formula is UNsatisfiable. So nondeterminism behaves fundamentally differently for space than for time — for space, guessing and its complement are equally powerful.

prompt: For a divide-and-conquer recurrence T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n), how do you read off the answer, and what is the intuition for the three cases?
reveal: Compare the work SPLITTING/combining, f(n), against the work at the LEAVES, n^(log_b a) (that exponent counts how fast the subproblems multiply). Case 1 — leaves dominate: if f(n) is polynomially smaller than n^(log_b a), then T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)); the cost piles up at the bottom of the recursion tree (e.g. a=8,b=2,f=n gives Θ(n^3)). Case 2 — balanced: if f(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a)), every level costs about the same, and with log n levels you get an extra log factor: T(n) = Θ(n^(log_b a) log n) — this is mergesort (a=2,b=2,f=n ⇒ Θ(n log n)). Case 3 — root dominates: if f(n) is polynomially larger (plus a regularity condition), the top-level combine swamps everything and T(n) = Θ(f(n)). The mental model is the recursion tree: total cost is the sum across levels, and the theorem just tells you whether that geometric series is bottom-heavy, flat, or top-heavy.
